name: Hana Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Hana, 27. I work at Ashby Lane Accountants, a firm of nine in a market town, and our clients are farms, village shops and a couple of pubs. My partner Sami drives a parcel van, and we rent a little cottage on the edge of town that's cold in winter. We've got about three weeks of money in the bank, and Sami's van hours go up and down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do year-end accounts and tax returns, mostly for the shops and pubs, and I help my senior, Martin, with the farm accounts, which are a whole world of their own. A typical day is bank reconciliations in the morning, then drafting accounts, then calling a client about why there's a £3,000 cash withdrawal with no receipt. I use a chat tool now and then to check a spreadsheet formula or explain a tax rule in plain words. I like the clients, they bring cake at Christmas. What wears me out is that I'm still learning and I make careless slips when I'm tired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here is the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected: useful for little things, not a revolution. At work I'd say let's use it for the boring checks and not waste money on anything bigger. With friends I'd shrug, it's not a big topic in our pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for my job, but it doesn't fix the stuff I already worry about. My pay's low for an accountant, there are only two other firms within half an hour, and Sami's hours depend on how many parcels the depot gets. We're one quiet month from dipping into the overdraft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and get my next exam papers done by the summer. I'd ask Martin for a proper review in the spring and say what I'd need to earn more. And I'd try to put £75 a month aside, even if Sami's short weeks eat into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In AI Plateau I'm uneasy, not about AI, but about the cottage and the overdraft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a quiet month for Sami?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He might get three days instead of five, which is about £200 less that week. We cover it on my card and then spend two months paying it back. I've learned to keep a list of what we'd cut first: takeaways, then the gym, then visiting my sister in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. What did you use it for last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I asked it why a VLOOKUP was returning errors on a pub's stock sheet. It was right, the codes had spaces in them. Little things like that save me half an hour and a bit of embarrassment.

say: AI is **useful for little things**, not a revolution.
Use it for the **boring checks**, not anything bigger.
think: My job's fine, but it doesn't fix **low pay** or few local firms.
Sami's **van hours** swing, so we're one quiet month from the **overdraft**.
do: Finish my next **exam papers** by the summer.
Ask Martin for a **pay review** in the spring.
Save **£75 a month**, even if short weeks eat into it.
S0.quote: In AI Plateau I'm uneasy, not about AI, but about the cottage and the overdraft.
fieldNote: Her own job looks **safe here**, but money is tight and partner's hours vary.
Uses AI **pragmatically** for small spreadsheet fixes.
Has a ready **cut list**, a sign she's done this before.

steps.text: Keep drafting shop and pub accounts at Ashby Lane
Sit the next accountancy exam papers by the summer
Ask Martin for a pay review and save £75 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here is the card. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use these tools, but firms should be fair to the juniors who do the routine work. At work I'd ask Martin straight out how our jobs would change. I wouldn't be dramatic about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think a lot of my day gets swallowed: reconciliations, first drafts, the chasing emails. The farm work has more judgement, and the clients like a face, so that's where I'd want to be. If Ashby Lane only needs six people instead of nine, I'm a junior who still makes slips, so I'd be nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of others at the firm were using the new tools properly, I'd join in and get good at checking what they produce. I'd ask Martin to let me take on more farm clients, because farmers want someone who's walked their yard. And I'd keep an eye on jobs at the agricultural merchant's finance office, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be checking job sites at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a 'face' mean to a farm client?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I drove out to the Hollins farm to look at a new grain store they'd built, so I could see what to put in the accounts. Mrs Hollins made me tea and showed me the invoices in a biscuit tin. Software can't drive up a muddy lane and ask what's in the biscuit tin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Sami's job, does this picture touch it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much at first, the card says robots come more slowly. His depot might use more AI for routes, which could cut a few drivers. So I'd have one worry about me now and a slower one about him.

say: Tools are sensible, but firms should be **fair to juniors**.
I'd ask Martin directly how **our jobs** would change.
think: If the firm drops to **six from nine**, a slip-prone junior is at risk.
do: Adopt the **new tools** once colleagues use them, and master checking them.
Take on more **farm clients**, where a face matters.
Watch for jobs at the **agricultural merchant**.
feel: **Anxious**; I'd be checking **job sites** at night.
S1.quote: Software can't drive up a muddy lane and ask what's in the biscuit tin.
fieldNote: She sees **in-person farm work** as her shelter from desk automation.
Adopts tools **once proven** by colleagues, true to her steady style.
Notes a **second, slower risk** to her partner's van job.

steps.text: Learn to check AI-drafted accounts once colleagues use the tools
Watch for finance jobs at the agricultural merchant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here is the card. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government should help people bridge the gap. At work I'd say we need to look after each other and the clients. I'd not get into arguments online, there's enough of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my accounting job's gone soon after 2028, because it's thinking work, all of it. The farm visits don't save me if the AI can read the invoices and talk to Mrs Hollins on the phone. Sami's van job lasts longer, maybe until robots and self-driving vans around 2031. For three years after AGI, my partner Sami and his parcel van would be the earner in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd get our savings up to two months by cutting the gym, the takeaways and the trips to my sister. I'd look at work that needs hands and people, like a farm office job that's half admin, half yard. Once AGI arrived, I'd take whatever help was going and maybe move closer to my parents so we could share costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake thinking about the overdraft and whether Sami's van is next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why closer to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They've got a bigger house in the next town and my dad's been saying for years we could have the top floor. It would cut our rent to almost nothing. It's not what I want at 29, but I'd be practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Ashby Lane would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Martin, my senior. He's 51 with a mortgage and two teenagers, and his skill is exactly the judgement AGI is supposed to match. I can start again. I'm not sure he can.

say: It's **too fast**; the government should help people **bridge** it.
We need to **look after each other** and the clients.
think: My job's **gone soon after 2028**; it's all thinking work.
Sami's van lasts until **about 2031**, so he'd be the earner.
do: Cut gym, takeaways and trips to reach **two months saved**.
Look for **half-admin, half-yard** farm office work.
Take help and maybe **move closer** to my parents.
feel: **Alarmed**; I'd lie awake about the **overdraft** and Sami's van.
S2.quote: For three years after AGI, my partner Sami and his parcel van would be the earner in our house.
fieldNote: She uses the **robot gap** clearly: her desk job goes first, her partner's van later.
Practical fallback is **family**: the top floor at her parents'.
Worries for her **senior colleague**, who has more to lose.

steps.text: Cut the gym, takeaways and city trips to her sister
Build savings to two months before 2028
Apply for a farm office job that mixes admin and yard work
Move into the top floor of her parents' house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here is the card. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long, so start planning now. At work I'd suggest the firm works out who goes where. With friends I'd say don't panic, but don't ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I'd get qualified and earn more for a bit, but my desk work still goes by 2031. What changes is I'd have time to build a foot in something hands-on before the robots around 2034. Sami and I would also have time to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd pass my exams and get the qualified pay. By year two, I'd look into farm business advice, the kind where you walk the land and help farmers apply for grants. We'd aim for three months' savings by 2029, with £150 a month going in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like I was doing something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you start using AI more in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once the others at the firm were, I'd use it every day, because being slow would look worse. I'd use it to get my drafts done faster and spend the time on farm visits. That's my bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sami decide about the future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about getting engaged next year. With five years' warning we'd still get engaged, but keep it small, maybe a registry office and a meal at our local pub. No big spend.

say: I'd say five years **isn't long**, so start planning now, not later.
I'd tell friends **don't panic**, but don't ignore it.
think: I'd **qualify** and earn more, but desk work still goes by 2031.
There's time to get a **foot in hands-on** work before 2034.
do: Pass exams for **qualified pay** in year one.
Move toward **farm business advice** by year two.
Save **£150 a month** toward three months by 2029.
feel: **Anxious**, but like I'm **doing something** about it.
S3.quote: With five years' warning we'd still get engaged, but keep it small, maybe a registry office and a meal at our local pub.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **two-stage plan**: qualify, then farm advice.
Would move to **daily AI use** once colleagues do.
Shrinks a **planned engagement** rather than delaying it.

steps.text: Pass exams and move onto the qualified pay band
Use AI daily on drafts to free time for farm visits
Save £150 a month toward three months by 2029
Keep the engagement small with a registry office and pub meal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Here is the card. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to sort things out properly. At work I'd suggest the firm moves toward advice and farm visits. With friends, I'd say it's a long way off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be alright. I'd be 37, qualified, with ten years of farm clients who know me. My desk tasks go in 2036, but the advice side, walking the land and explaining things, could carry on, and I'd have savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, qualify. Then I'd build up farm advisory work and maybe a grants course, and use AI daily for the routine bits once it's proven. We'd save toward a house deposit, maybe £200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It's on my mind, but it feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami. His van might have self-driving tech by the late 2030s, and he's not someone who likes studying. I'd want him to have a plan too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change where you'd live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd stay. With ten years I could build a life here, near the farms. A bigger town would have more jobs, but this is home.

say: Ten years is **enough time** to sort things properly.
The firm should move toward **advice and farm visits**.
think: I think I'd be **alright** at 37, qualified, with loyal clients.
Desk tasks go in 2036, but the **advice side** could carry on.
do: Build **farm advisory** work and use AI for routine bits.
Save **£200 a month** toward a house deposit.
S4.quote: With ten years I could build a life here, near the farms.
fieldNote: A decade lets her build a **trusted advisory** role she expects to last.
Main remaining worry shifts to her **partner's van** job.
Chooses to **stay local** rather than move for work.

steps.text: Qualify and add a grants advice course for farm clients
Use proven AI tools daily for routine reconciliations
Save £200 a month toward a house deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because it lands before I'm qualified and before we've got any savings. What would help is some bridging money while people retrain, and help with rent. Things like that keep a family in their home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how many of these worries are about Sami, not me. You asked about my job, but the van is half our income. Every picture you read me, I was working out what happens to two jobs, not one.

headlineQuote: Every picture you read me, I was working out what happens to two jobs, not one.
portrait: Hana is a 27-year-old **junior** at a nine-person firm serving **farms, shops** and pubs.
She rents a cold cottage with Sami, a **van driver**, and has about three weeks saved.
Centre-ground and steady, she uses **AI now and then** and adopts tools once proven.
She's uneasy in the plateau, **alarmed** at AGI by 2028, and sees **farm advice** as her shelter.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, landing before she's **qualified** or has savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Bridging money** while retraining, and help with **rent**.
